sentences.text: 1. The appellant is aggrieved by judgment dated 09.02.2010 passed by the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan at Jodhpur, whereby her appeal against the award of the Reference Court dated 23.09.1994, as well as the cross appeal preferred by respondent-Rajasthan State Industrial Development and Investment Corporation (in short RIICO), have been dismissed upholding the grant of compensation for the acquired land @ 5250/- per bigha.

entities.label: COURT

entities.label: RESPONDENT

sentences.text: FACTS 2.

The State of Rajasthan issued a notification on 03.07.1980 under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act (in short Act) for acquiring land measuring 376 bigha 5 biswa situated in Chak Shyam Singh Wala, District Sri Ganganagar for RIICO.
It was followed by a notification 17:21:53 IST under Section 6 of the Act.
The possession of the acquired land was taken on 09.12.1982.
The land acquisition officer passed the award on 06.07.1983 granting compensation at 3500 per bigha.

3. It may be mentioned that the appellant had purchased land measuring 17 bigha 1 biswa by way of four registered sale deeds executed on different dates in April 1979 (Annexure A1 to A4 of IA No.42306 of 2022) situated in Chak Shyam Singh Wala.
Even before the said land could be mutated in the name of the appellant, the same got acquired by way of the abovementioned acquisition process.
The compensation for appellants land was also, thus, awarded by the land acquisition officer @ 3500/- per bigha.
4. The appellant moved an application on 05.08.1983 before the land acquisition officer seeking a reference under Section 18 of the Act.

It appears that the said application was initially rejected being Suman Setia vs Raj.State Indusl.Dev.& Inv.Corp. on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/14853485/
1 not maintainable as the appellant was not recorded as owner of the acquired land but, after a protracted round of litigation which went upto the High Court, the matter was eventually referred to the Reference Court for adjudication of the appellants claim.

sentences.text: 5. The Reference Court passed an award on 23.09.1994 granting compensation @ 5250/- per bigha.

The award of the Reference Court noted that  (a) the appellant was not entitled to claim compensation at the rate on which the RIICO sold the developed industrial plots; (b) the value of the land has been increasing continuously and there was more than 50% increase in the last three years;
(c) the appellants land was non-agricultural land; (d) the appellant was not entitled to compensation for the 40 quarters allegedly constructed at the site; (e) the appellant was entitled to statutory benefits like solatium and interest as per the law.
6. The appellant as well as RIICO both challenged the award of the Reference Court but as noticed in the opening paragraph of this order, the respective challenges were turned down by the High Court.
7.
It also appears from the record that the appellant purchased the land from one Avtar Singh s/o Bakhtawar Singh.

The said Avtar Singh had applied to the District Collector Sri Ganganagar to grant Change of Land Use mainly to convert the agricultural land for non- agricultural purposes and his application was allowed by the Collector Sri Ganganagar vide order dated 18.09.1975 to the extent of land measuring 4 bigha 19 biswa only.
The said converted land was also part of the land measuring 17 bigha 1 biswa purchased by the appellant.
SUBMISSIONS 8.

In the factual backdrop that the High Court has accepted the rate of compensation assessed by the Reference Court, Mr. P.S. Patwalia, learned senior counsel for the appellant vehemently urges that there is a plethora of documentary evidence on record to establish that the value of the acquired land, at the relevant time, was not less than 9000-10000/- per bigha.
In this regard, learned senior counsel has drawn our attention, firstly to the award dated 06.07.1983 passed by the Land Acquisition Officer.
It may be noted that no exemplar of any land sold in Chak Shaym Singh Wala where the acquired land was located, was available.
Hence, no sale instance was available in respect of the land in Chak Shyam Singh Wala.

The land acquisition officer, therefore, sought a report from the Sub-Registrar, who vide letter dated 02.05.1983 firstly gave instances of three sale deeds of Chak 11 LNP, four instances of Chak 12 LNP and three instances of Chaks 13 and 14 LNP, which may be summarised in a tabulated form, as follows:

The land acquisition officer then referred to a report dated 11.11.1982 sent by the Revenue Patwari opining that the value of uncommand land (unirrigated land) of Chak Shyam Singh Wala was 10,000/- per bigha.

This report, it appears, was based upon a sale instance of Chak 8 ML for a land measuring 2 bigha, which according to the land acquisition officer was a small area and was otherwise located in Chak of Sadulshahar Tehsil i.e. approximately 5 kms. away from the acquired land.

10. As regard to the photocopy of a sale deed produced by the land owners, the land acquisition officer noted that it pertained to an uncommand area of Chak 6 LLG Tehsil Sadulshahar where the land was sold @ 6500/- per bigha.
This instance was also not relied upon keeping in view its distance from the acquired land.

Another sale instance of 4 bigha command land sold @ 10,000/-
per bigha in Chak 13 LNPII too was discarded being not situated near the acquired land.

The land acquisition officer in the penultimate discussion held that if all the sale instances of nearby Chaks,
referred to above are taken together, the rate of the land was between 7000/- to 8000/- per bigha.

He then held that the market rate of uncommand land is invariably 40% to 60% less than the command land and after applying that cut, the land owners were held entitled to compensation @
3500/- per bigha.

11. Learned senior counsel for the appellant, thus, submits that there was no rationale behind imposing the cut of nearly 60% by the land acquisition officer when it was proved from the sale instances of nearby Chaks that the rate of the acquired land was somewhere 7000/- to 8000/-
per bigha.

He has made a pointed reference to the location of the acquired land which is abutted to Hanumangarh - Sri Ganganagar Highway and, thus, carried better potentiality as compared to the sale instances referred to above, for industrial or commercial purposes.
He urges that a part of the land had already been changed for non-agricultural purposes, therefore, also it was incorrect to evaluate the acquired land as an agricultural land.

sentences.text: Learned senior counsel then refers to the award passed by the Reference Court, wherein it is observed that the appellant had purchased the land for a sale consideration of 65,000/- in April 1979 and, hence, she was entitled to approximate increase of 50% or more over the said land.
Consequently, the Reference Court enhanced the compensation to 5250/- per bigha.

According to him, the Reference Court fell in error, firstly, by ignoring the sale instances according to which the rate in the surrounding areas was not less than 7000/- to 8000/- per bigha and; secondly,
despite having been proved on record that the appellant had constructed 40 quarters on the acquired land, her claim for grant of compensation @ 3000/- per quarter was erroneously turned down.

13. Lastly, learned senior counsel has placed heavy reliance on a subsequent award dated 20.03.1998 passed by the Reference Court in respect of the adjoining land owned by the appellants husband, for which compensation has been granted @ approximately 18,000/- per bigha, besides additional compensation for the running brick kiln and investments made by the appellants husband in establishment of an industrial unit.
He submits that the above-stated award was unsuccessfully challenged before the High Court and the same has attained finality between the parties.

The land of the appellants husband was also acquired vide the same acquisition process and hence, it is urged, the above-stated award, a copy of which has been placed on record by way of additional documents, is the best exemplar to assess the market value of the appellants land.
14. In contrast, Dr. Manish Singhvi, learned senior counsel for RIICO vehemently opposes the claim of the appellant.
He submits, at the outset, that the best exemplar in the case is sale deeds of the appellant herself when she purchased the land for a total consideration of 65,000/- a year before the acquisition.

He urges that even applying the principle of annual escalation, there could be an addition of not more than 10-20% in the said sale price but the Reference Court has granted 53%
enhancement to the appellant.

Learned senior counsel, maintains that the sale instances, noted in extenso by the land Acquisition Officer, cannot be relied upon to determine the market value in the instant case for the reasons that  (a) most of the sale instances are after issuance of notification under Section 4 of the Act on 03.07.1980; (b) none of the sale deed pertains to Chak Shaym Singh Wala; (c) these sale instances are mostly located 5 kms. away from the acquired land; (d) most of the sale instances are of command land i.e. irrigated land, whereas the land of the appellant has been found to be uncommand land i.e. non-irrigated.
ANALYSIS 15.
We have considered the rival submissions made on behalf of the parties and perused the material placed on record.
16. Firstly, we may deal with the subsequent award dated 20.03.1998 (Annexure A/10 of I.A No.42306 of 2022) passed by the Reference Court in the case of land of the appellants husband.
The said award, in our considered opinion, does not assist us in evaluation of fair and just price of the appellants land.

We say so for the reason, that the land owned by the appellants husband was admittedly being used for non-agricultural purposes and there was a running industrial unit of brick kiln operating at the site.

A perusal of the above-stated award reveals that overwhelming Suman Setia vs Raj.State Indusl.Dev.& Inv.Corp. on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/14853485/
4

sentences.text: documentary evidence was led to establish that the partnership firm, namely, the owner of the land was running the brick kiln and as such the land was not to be assessed as an agricultural land.

On the other hand, there is not an iota of evidence to suggest that the appellants land was being used for non- agricultural purposes except for the 40 quarters that were said to have been constructed over the said land.
There is no gain to say that there will be a distinction between the market value of the non- agricultural/industrial land as compared to the agricultural land.

Secondly, the reasons assigned by the Reference Court for awarding compensation at a higher rate to the firm of the appellants husband are conspicuously missing in terms of evidence or arguments in the case in hand.
There is also no proof that both the lands are of same potentiality or value.
Thus, it would be not safe to place reliance on the subsequent award and to grant higher compensation to the appellant based thereupon.

17. Adverting to the sale instances relied upon by the land owners as well as those, details of which were obtained by the land Acquisition Officer from the office of Sub-Registrar, it is not in dispute that no relevant sale instance in respect of the land of Chak Shaym Singh Wala was available.
In such circumstances, the best exemplars could be the sale instances of the lands of adjoining chaks.

It may be further seen from the details of such sale instances, as reproduced in tabulated form in paragraph 8 of this order, only two sale instances were before Section 4 notification was issued on 03.07.1980.

Even if the sale instances, which were executed near the same time period are also taken into consideration, what emerges out is that the rate of the land in the nearby vicinity was somewhere between 7000/- to 8000/- per bigha.
It is true that some of the sale instances pertained to command land, particularly both the sale instances which were prior to issuance of Section 4 notification.

Since the fact that the land has been acquired for development of the industrial area, the factum of the land being command or non-command alone may not the crucial factor for assessment of its market value.
The land of the appellant was located on the main highway i.e. Hanumangarh  Sri Ganganagar Road and thus has high potentiality to utilise for industrialization.
We, however, agree with Dr. Singhvi that a parcel of command land will definitely have an edge over the uncommand land.
We may also, at this stage, refer to the report sent by Area Patwari valuing the uncommand land of Chak Shaym Singh Wala @ 10,000/- per bigha.
It appears that the said report was based upon a sale instance of a small area of 2 bigha land.

After imposing a suitable cut towards development charges, coupled with the estimated market value discernible from other sale instances of adjoining Chaks, it appears to us that the fair market value of the land of the appellant was not less than 6500/- per bigha at the relevant time.
CONCLUSION 18.

Keeping in view the peculiar location of the appellants land and facts and circumstances of this case, the appellant is held entitled for compensation @ 6500/- per bigha including all the statutory benefits.
Ordered accordingly.
19. So far as the appellants claim for compensation for alleged quarters is concerned, there is a concurrent finding of fact that no such quarters were found in existence.
we are thus not inclined to entertain such claim, which is accordingly rejected.
